scenario: A platform team at Contoso is setting up a new generative AI initiative in Azure AI Foundry and needs to decide how to structure their workspace before onboarding multiple product teams.
question: Which Azure AI Foundry resource type provides a single, unified project experience with simplified default network and identity configuration, recommended for teams starting a new project today?
options: A Foundry project (Azure AI Foundry resource)
explanation: The newer Foundry project (backed by an Azure AI Foundry resource) is Microsoft's recommended starting point — it bundles the endpoint, keys, and default connections in one resource with simpler defaults. Hub-based projects still exist for scenarios needing shared connections/compute across multiple projects, but are no longer the default recommendation for new single-team projects. A plain Azure ML workspace or Cognitive Services multi-service resource lacks the Foundry-specific project experience (playground, agent service, evaluation).

scenario: A developer wants to evaluate several LLMs — an Azure OpenAI model, a Meta Llama model, and a Cohere model — before committing to one for a new chatbot.
question: Where in Azure AI Foundry can the developer browse and compare these models from multiple providers side by side?
explanation: The model catalog is the central hub for browsing first-party (Azure OpenAI, Phi), partner, and open-source models (Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere, DeepSeek, and more), including benchmarks, licensing, and supported deployment options for each. Azure AI Search is a retrieval/indexing service, Content Safety Studio is for moderation configuration, and Azure Monitor is for observability — none browse or compare models.

scenario: A team wants to deploy Mistral-Large from the model catalog without provisioning or managing any virtual machines, paying only for the tokens they consume.
question: Which deployment option should they choose?
options: Managed compute (real-time endpoint on a dedicated VM)
explanation: Serverless API deployment (model-as-a-service) hosts many catalog models — including Mistral, Meta Llama, and Cohere families — on Microsoft-managed infrastructure with consumption-based, pay-per-token billing and no customer-managed compute. Managed compute requires provisioning and paying for a dedicated VM-backed endpoint regardless of usage. PTU is an Azure OpenAI-specific reserved-capacity option, not a generic catalog deployment mode.

scenario: A financial-services customer needs a deployment of GPT-4o with guaranteed, consistent low latency for a real-time trading assistant and is willing to commit to reserved capacity.
question: Which Azure OpenAI deployment type best fits this requirement?
explanation: Provisioned throughput (PTU) reserves dedicated model capacity for a customer, delivering predictable, consistent latency and throughput — ideal for latency-sensitive production workloads willing to commit to reserved units. Standard and Global Standard are shared, pay-as-you-go capacity with variable latency under load. Global Batch is for large, non-latency-sensitive asynchronous jobs processed within a 24-hour window at a discount.

scenario: A developer is building a RAG chatbot in Azure AI Foundry and needs the project to retrieve passages from a private knowledge base at query time.
question: What must the developer add to the Foundry project to enable this retrieval-augmented generation pattern?
options: A connection to an Azure AI Search resource with a populated vector/hybrid index
A second Azure OpenAI deployment for redundancy
explanation: RAG requires an external index the model can query for grounding context — in Azure AI Foundry this is typically an Azure AI Search connection with a vector or hybrid index built over the private documents. Extra model deployments don't provide retrieval; Content Safety and Prompt Shields address moderation and injection defense, not grounding.

scenario: A developer writing Python automation needs to programmatically list deployments and manage connections in a Foundry project, separate from making inference calls to a deployed model.
question: Which SDK is purpose-built for this project- and resource-management task, as distinct from the SDK used for chat/embedding calls?
explanation: azure-ai-projects is the Azure AI Foundry SDK for management-plane operations — listing connections, deployments, agents, and datasets within a project. azure-ai-inference (or the OpenAI SDK pointed at a Foundry endpoint) is used for the data-plane inference calls (chat completions, embeddings) themselves. azure-storage-blob is unrelated to Foundry project management.

scenario: A team wants to fine-tune a base model on their own labeled support-ticket conversations to improve response tone and format.
question: What format must the training data file use when submitting a fine-tuning job in Azure AI Foundry?
options: A CSV file with two columns: prompt and completion
A JSONL file where each line is a conversation object with a messages array of role/content pairs
A plain .txt file with one example per paragraph
A Parquet file exported from Azure AI Search
explanation: Fine-tuning jobs expect a JSONL file, one JSON object per line, each containing a messages array (system/user/assistant turns) matching the chat-completion message format — mirroring how the model will be used in production. CSV, plain text, and Parquet are not accepted training-data formats for this pipeline.

scenario: An architect is estimating throughput limits before load-testing a new Azure OpenAI deployment.
question: Which two quota dimensions does Azure OpenAI enforce per deployment to control capacity consumption?
options: Number of connections and number of projects
explanation: Azure OpenAI quota is expressed and enforced in tokens-per-minute (TPM) and requests-per-minute (RPM) per deployment, and these can be adjusted (within subscription limits) or split across multiple deployments. The other options are infrastructure metrics that aren't how Azure OpenAI quota is modeled.

scenario: A prompt engineer wants to quickly iterate on a system message and a couple of few-shot examples before writing any application code.
question: Which Azure AI Foundry feature is designed for this rapid, code-free iteration?
explanation: The chat playground lets you adjust the system message, parameters (temperature, top-p), and try few-shot examples interactively, then view the equivalent code/JSON to carry into your app — no code required for the iteration itself. The other options are for evaluation, building agents programmatically, and observability, respectively — later stages of the workflow.

scenario: A platform team is deciding between a hub-based project (shared across three product teams) and separate Foundry projects for each team.
question: What is the primary architectural benefit of a hub in this scenario?
options: It removes the need for any network security configuration
It centralizes shared connections, compute, and security boundaries that multiple child projects can reuse
It automatically merges all teams' data into one fine-tuned model
It exempts the workspace from content filtering requirements
explanation: A hub acts as the shared container for connections (Azure AI Search, storage, Key Vault), compute, and networking/security configuration that multiple projects underneath it can inherit — useful when several teams need consistent governance without reconfiguring each project. It doesn't remove security needs, merge data automatically, or bypass content filtering.

scenario: Before committing to a model for a cost-sensitive, high-volume summarization feature, a team wants to compare quality, latency, and cost trade-offs across several catalog models.
question: Which model catalog feature directly supports this comparison?
explanation: Model benchmarks in the catalog show comparative quality, cost, and throughput/latency metrics across models on standard datasets, helping teams shortlist candidates before deployment. The other listed features relate to safety configuration and agent conversation state, not model comparison.

scenario: A compliance reviewer asks whether a team deploying GPT-4o in Azure AI Foundry can turn off all content filtering to allow unrestricted outputs for an internal red-teaming exercise.
question: What is true about default content filtering on Azure OpenAI deployments in Azure AI Foundry?
options: Content filters are optional add-ons and off by default
Content filters are enabled by default and can only be modified or disabled after approval via the Limited Access review process
Content filters can be freely disabled by any project owner at any time
Content filters only apply to image-generation models, not text models
explanation: Azure OpenAI deployments have default content filters enabled; modifying severity thresholds or disabling filtering (e.g., for approved red-teaming) requires applying for and being approved under Microsoft's Limited Access / modified content filtering process — it isn't a self-service toggle. Filters apply to both text and image models where supported.

scenario: A team wants to visually chain a retrieval step, a prompt template, and an LLM call, then bulk-test the chain against 200 sample questions before deploying it as an endpoint.
question: Which Azure AI Foundry capability is purpose-built for this visual chaining and bulk evaluation?
explanation: Prompt flow provides a visual, DAG-based authoring canvas for chaining retrieval, prompt, and LLM/code nodes, plus built-in bulk-test and evaluate runs and one-click deployment to a managed endpoint. The model catalog is for model selection, the AI Search indexer is for data ingestion, and Content Safety Studio configures moderation — none author or bulk-test chains.

scenario: A team based in a region where a newly released frontier model isn't yet listed as deployable discovers their deployment attempt fails.
question: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Azure AI Foundry requires a support ticket for every deployment
Model availability in the catalog is region-specific, and the model may not yet be offered in that region/deployment type
All models are globally available immediately upon catalog release
explanation: Catalog models — especially newly released ones — roll out to specific Azure regions and specific deployment types (serverless API vs. managed compute vs. Azure OpenAI SKUs) incrementally, not globally and instantly. Checking the model card's region/deployment availability is the standard troubleshooting step, not filing a ticket or assuming subscription issues.

scenario: An architect explaining Azure AI Foundry to a new hire summarizes the platform's core value proposition.
question: Which statement best captures what Azure AI Foundry unifies into a single platform?
options: Only image-generation models and their licensing terms
Model selection/deployment, agent orchestration, evaluation, and responsible-AI tooling in one connected workflow
Exclusively Azure Machine Learning's classical ML pipeline designer
A replacement for Azure Active Directory identity management
explanation: Azure AI Foundry's value is bringing together model catalog/deployment, the Agent Service for building and orchestrating agents, prompt flow, evaluation, tracing, and responsible-AI/content-safety tooling into one connected project experience — spanning the generative-AI app lifecycle, not just one model type or classical ML. It is not an identity platform (that's Microsoft Entra ID).
